source_refs.note: 2. Disaccharides: a main subheading of 27.1 Carbohydrates, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 161-161.

blocks.text: Disaccharides consist of two monosaccharide units joined together via glycosidic linkage, generally with the formula C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁. Among the most common disaccharides are sucrose, lactose and maltose. They are formed through a condensation reaction, when the hydroxyl group of one monosaccharide combines with the hydrogen of another monosaccharide through a covalent bond, releasing a molecule of water. The bond C–O–C is known as the glycosidic bond. For example, sucrose which is a common table sugar, is a disaccharide of glucose and fructose as given in Figure 27.2.

blocks.alt: In one row from left to right: glucose (six-membered ring) and fructose (five-membered ring) drawn as Haworth rings; the H of the OH on glucose C1 and the HO on fructose C2 are boxed. A horizontal arrow leads to sucrose, in which C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose are joined through one oxygen atom, labelled 'glycosidic linkage in sucrose', + H2O.
